title: KFC to switch to Coca-Cola beverages in U.S. restaurants for the first time in decades
description: KFC's U.S. restaurants will ditch PepsiCo and switch to Coca-Cola beverages next year, marking the first time in decades that the Yum Brands chain has
body: KFC's U.S. restaurants will ditch PepsiCo and switch to Coca-Cola beverages next year, marking the first time in decades that the Yum Brands chain has changed its drink supplier, the restaurant company said Thursday.Some of KFC's international markets serve Coke products, but the chain's U.S. restaurants have stuck with PepsiCo drinks ever since Pepsi bought KFC in 1986. At the time of the acquisition, KFC was Coke's second-largest fountain account, trailing only McDonald's. Pepsi later spun off KFC, along with sister chains Pizza Hut and Taco Bell — but even as the combined Yum Brands, the company stayed loyal to its previous owner. Without Pepsi, Taco Bell would not serve its iconic Mountain Dew Baja Blast.The change comes as KFC aims to win back U.S. diners, who have ditched the fried chicken chain for rivals such as Chick-fil-A or Popeyes. "This decision is a critical step in the Kentucky Fried Comeback," KFC U.S. President Catherine Tan-Gillespie wrote in a memo to franchisees and employees obtained by CNBC. "A new beverage offering, with a new partner in Coca-Cola, gives us a platform to innovate, meet changing tastes and give customers more reasons to choose us."Beverage cups stacked inside a Yum Brands KFC restaurant in Shelbyville, Kentucky, Jan. 29, 2021.Luke Sharrett | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesFor many fast-food chains, beverages have become a critical way to attract consumers. A number of restaurants, including McDonald's and Taco Bell, have broadened their drink offerings with options such as refreshers or "dirty soda." For its part, KFC recently unveiled new drinks, including iced coffees and shakes, at Open House, its innovation restaurant in McKinney, Texas. Coke told CNBC earlier this year that the company has helped many of its restaurant partners create new drinks.KFC expects to be pouring Coke beverages in all of its U.S. restaurants by the end of the first quarter of 2027, Tan-Gillespie said.Tan-Gillespie also said that Pepsi remains an important partner for KFC's parent company and the chain's international markets.For decades, Coke and Pepsi have tussled over important restaurant partners, which represent both a sales opportunity and the chance to grow the visibility of their beverage brands. It is unusual for large restaurant chains to switch beverage providers, but not unprecedented. In 2024, Pepsi poached Subway, the largest U.S. restaurant chain by number of locations, from Coke. Besides KFC, Coke has wooed away a number of notable Pepsi customers in recent years, including Culver's, Arby's and Panda Express.

schema.headline: KFC to switch to Coca-Cola beverages in U.S. restaurants for the first time in decades

title: Prediction market odds on Tesla-SpaceX merger are above 50% for early 2027
description: Tesla CEO Elon Musk during a state dinner in the East Room of the White House in Washington, Sept. 24, 2026.Annabelle Gordon | Bloomberg | Getty Image
body: Tesla CEO Elon Musk during a state dinner in the East Room of the White House in Washington, Sept. 24, 2026.Annabelle Gordon | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesFollowing a Barclays note Wednesday that outlined what a merger between Tesla and SpaceX could look like, prediction market traders increased the odds of an integration above 50% for early 2027.Odds of a merger happening before March jumped to 56% by Friday morning, up from 29%. Odds for an integration before April and May climbed to similar levels. The contract asks, "When will Tesla and SpaceX merge?" and will be verified by news outlets and the Securities and Exchange Commission's EDGAR database. Tesla, known for its electric vehicles, and SpaceX, a rocket and satellite company, have collaborated before. Both are controlled by Elon Musk. On Thursday, Tesla showed off its long-delayed Roadster, which relies on SpaceX technology to make the vehicle hover. A video showcasing the Roadster's capabilities was also recorded from SpaceX's test site in Texas.Beyond collaboration, the growing speculation of a merger comes after Musk spoke of "more and more overlap" between Tesla and SpaceX on the EV maker's latest earnings call. Barclays now expects a merger could be announced before Tesla's annual general meeting, which must take place no later than Dec. 6, 2026. Analyst Dan Levy expects the merger may be proposed as an AI vertical integration, involving Tesla's Robotaxi and Optimus with SpaceX's Grok and Macrohard. Terafab, the semiconductor project relying on Tesla, SpaceX and xAI, could also be a "key driver" for the merger, Levy added. "Notably, while we suspect there would be some financial synergies, the true value would be in vertical integration," Levy said. Earlier Friday, Evercore ISI recommended buying SpaceX shares ahead of its next scheduled earnings release, set for early November, and boosted its 12-month price target on the stock by 20% to $275.Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

schema.headline: Prediction market odds on Tesla-SpaceX merger are above 50% for early 2027

title: U.S. presses China on Mastercard, Citigroup market access in bilateral Bangkok talks, official says
description: A Citibank branch in New York, US, on Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026.Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesBANGKOK – U.S. officials pressed Beijing on market
body: A Citibank branch in New York, US, on Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026.Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesBANGKOK – U.S. officials pressed Beijing on market access issues for Mastercard Inc and Citigroup Inc during at least two bilateral meetings with Chinese counterparts in Bangkok this week, according to a U.S. Treasury official. The Treasury delegation, led by Deputy Secretary Francis Brooke, held bilateral meetings with officials from the People's Bank of China and the finance ministry on the sidelines of the Group of 20 finance meetings and the IMF-World Bank annual gathering this week, the official said, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss the closed-door meetings.The talks included market access for U.S. companies, including Mastercard, Visa and Citigroup, the official said, adding that regulatory approval was part of the agreement reached during the meeting between Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping during the latter's state visit in Washington last month.The sideline meetings in Bangkok continued discussions on implementing these deals, the official said. The PBOC, China's National Financial Regulatory Administration, China Securities Regulatory Commission, Chinese embassies in Singapore and Thailand, the U.S. Treasury Department press office and Visa did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment. Citigroup and Mastercard declined to comment.The progress follows China's Oct. 13 approval for Visa Inc. to begin preparing a wholly owned domestic card-clearing business. Visa has up to a year to prepare before it applies for an operating license, the PBOC has said.China has opened much of its financial sector to foreign firms since 2018, gradually lifting foreign ownership caps on services such as securities, futures and fund management. It still limits cross-border capital flows and has kept state-backed domestic players dominant in payments. Mastercard currently operates yuan card payments in China through a local joint venture with NetsUnion Clearing Corp., which began operating in 2024. The pending approval would allow it to operate as an independent entity, the person said. Citigroup — which has hired several dozen employees for its China unit — is seeking a wholly owned securities license to conduct A-share brokerage, underwriting, research and principal trading businesses in the onshore market, two people familiar with the industry said, requesting anonymity for discussing private matters. One of the two people close to Citigroup said the bank planned to increase its China securities staff to about 100. The bank applied in late 2021, and Reuters reported last month that approval could come soon. Trump and Xi are expected to meet in person for the third time this year in Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in November. "The move suggests the US-China trade environment remains benign, and Beijing is keen to keep up the momentum," said Dan Wang, China director at Eurasia Group. Licensing U.S. financial firms is a "limited concession" on market access, she said, though it signals China is continuing to open up, and "this should marginally bolster investor confidence in Chinese assets."

schema.headline: U.S. presses China on Mastercard, Citigroup market access in bilateral Bangkok talks, official says

title: Analysis: Why a $2 trillion deficit and 5% Treasury yields are becoming America's biggest economic challenge
description: A "For Sale" sign outside a single-family home in Carlsbad, California, U.S., Sept. 16, 2026. Mike Blake | ReutersLong-term bond yields above 5% and a
body: A "For Sale" sign outside a single-family home in Carlsbad, California, U.S., Sept. 16, 2026. Mike Blake | ReutersLong-term bond yields above 5% and a $2 trillion deficit are giving Americans a taste of what a U.S. debt crisis would be like. A true emergency would hurt much more, and isn't baked in. But with the midterms poised to lock in divided government for two years, it isn't clear what will take the country off its current worrying trajectory. Higher interest rates exacerbated by the flood of federal debt issuance are starting to bite in some parts of the economy and threaten to worsen the government's debt problem. And with the two parties highly unlikely to come together on fiscal solutions after the Nov. 3 midterms, any fixes are years off in the future. The housing market is showing signs of slowing as the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage hovers around 7.5%. Pending home sales fell 4% in September, Redfin said Monday, the biggest monthly drop in three years. Mortgage rates track the 10-year Treasury yield. The 10-year has climbed 114 basis points, or hundredths of a percentage point, since the end of February through midday Friday, when the 10-year traded at 5.1%.Several factors are pushing up the 10-year, including the war with Iran, which kicked off on Feb. 28 and precipitated the rise in long-term yields. Oil and diesel prices are up sharply, and that has bond traders asking for more yield to account for the possibility that central banks such as the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates. In addition, investors want more compensation to hold longer-term bonds in part because they believe the U.S. government will continue to flood the market with them. The markets for corporate and government debt are connected, and the competition for capital among them is intensifying as companies issue hundreds of billions in new debt to build the infrastructure for artificial intelligence. Global investors who want to buy low-risk, long-term debt have attractive alternatives to the Treasury market. If the U.S. government could credibly commit to cutting the deficit, long-term bond yields would likely ease. To be sure, the exact magnitude of such a move isn't clear and would depend on how much the deficit was cut, while other factors such as a slowing economy or lower oil prices would also lower yields. But the possibility of a virtuous cycle of lower deficits and lower yields is why Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has argued that the U.S. ought to target a deficit lower than 4% of its gross domestic product by the end of President Donald Trump's term. There is almost no way the U.S. will hit that target. The deficit was $1.992 trillion for the 2026 fiscal year, up 12% from last year, data released Friday by the U.S. Treasury showed. That deficit amounts to approximately 6.2% of gross domestic product, based on an estimate of third-quarter GDP. Higher rates make debt reduction tougher. If interest rates stay a half-point above the CBO's expectations, the cumulative deficit over 10 years will come in $1.9 trillion higher, the agency estimates. If rates overshoot by 1.5 points, that adds $6 trillion in deficits. The CBO expects the 10-year Treasury to average 4.3% over that period, compared with 5.1% today. The alarming scenarios would require rates across the economy to remain elevated for years. "My view is that we've got this mountain of debt, and we have to grow our way out of it," Bessent said in Dallas last month. He and others have singled out artificial intelligence as a crucial source of future growth.AI could help but can't fix the problem entirely. It would take a decade of 7.2% growth to balance the budget with growth alone, according to the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, a research group that advocates for balanced budgets. GDP growth was recently revised up for the second quarter from 1.5% to 2.2% at an annualized rate. The acceleration that quickly would get us to 7.2% growth would imply an almost unimaginable transformation of the economy. Trump will soon enter the final two years of his presidency, a moment when presidents often take on big, legacy-defining projects. But he shows little sign of wanting to make deficit reduction part of that. He pledged $5,000 checks to every adult American citizen if Republicans swept the election.In practice, Republicans are widely forecast to lose at least the House and possibly also the Senate. Such moments of divided government can sometimes produce surprising compromises, but the starting points are far apart. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, Democrats' likely next House speaker, wants to reverse the $1 trillion in healthcare cuts that Congress enacted last year as part of Trump's signature legislative package. And that's leaving aside the deep animosity between the parties. The overall U.S. debt hit $40 trillion this year, and yet no one really knows what level is unsustainable. A full-on debt crisis likely remains much further out in the future. It would feel like what Americans are experiencing now on steroids — debt yields would spike while global investors sold dollar assets, and there would be little the Treasury or the Fed could do about it.For now, though higher yields are also attracting investors to U.S. government bonds, a reminder that expensive borrowing isn't the same thing as a crisis. But the bottom line is that economics alone can't solve the problem. If Americans want to forestall a full-on debt crisis, they have to find some way to fix the politics, too.

schema.headline: Analysis: Why a $2 trillion deficit and 5% Treasury yields are becoming America's biggest economic challenge

title: Semiconductor market to remain solid ‘at least through next year,’ South Korea finance minister says
description: South Korean Finance Minister nominee Lee Hyoung-il speaks during his confirmation hearing at the National Assembly in Seoul, South Korea, Sept. 15, 2
body: South Korean Finance Minister nominee Lee Hyoung-il speaks during his confirmation hearing at the National Assembly in Seoul, South Korea, Sept. 15, 2026.Kim Hong-ji | ReutersThe semiconductor boom will last at least through 2027, South Korean finance minister Lee Hyoung-Il said on Saturday. "For now, our view is that we can sustain this growth at least through next year," Lee told CNBC on the sidelines of the IMF-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok. "That's because the gap between demand and supply for semiconductors is still very wide, and supply is still being expanded."His comments come after semiconductor stocks fell sharply this week, hurt by investor concerns about interest rate hikes and rising competition from Chinese companies. South Korean chip stocks like SK Hynix and Seoul Semiconductor were part of the sell-off, along with U.S. giants like Nvidia.Chip stocks have fueled volatility in South Korea's stock market this year, Lee said. He attributed the market's wild swings to the semiconductor industry's larger share of the economy than in other countries. Despite the market swings, South Korea's economy is "solid," Lee said.On Thursday, an opinion column in Maeil Business Newspaper, a prominent South Korean publication, urged the country's government to prepare for the coming slowdown in the artificial intelligence boom. The author said two experts expect a "flood of new supply" of semiconductors that will turn the memory market "into a red ocean" by 2029, according to a CNBC translation.Read more CNBC tech newsApple's $1,999 iPhone Duo puts the company's status-symbol power to the testTrump says White House didn't order Starlink restrictions in UkraineBlue Origin plans $330 million Florida expansion to ramp New Glenn launchesSpaceX AI policy leader grilled by NYC Council on Grok safety, sexualized imagesWhile South Korea's semiconductors may be driving volatility in its stock market, the industry has also fueled tax growth. Lee said the country expects to collect more taxes than initially projected this year. South Korea will ultimately be in a stronger fiscal position because of the chip boom, he added.WATCH: Don't overlook opportunity in South Korea, says Verdad Advisers' Rasmussenwatch now

schema.headline: Semiconductor market to remain solid ‘at least through next year,’ South Korea finance minister says

title: Trump waives broad new Russia sanctions and tariffs under Graham Act, citing national interest
description: U.S. President Donald Trump welcomes Russian President Vladimir Putin to Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson on Aug. 15, 2025, in Anchorage, Alaska.Contri
body: U.S. President Donald Trump welcomes Russian President Vladimir Putin to Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson on Aug. 15, 2025, in Anchorage, Alaska.Contributor | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesPresident Donald Trump signed an executive order late Friday waiving parts of a recently enacted package of sanctions aimed at curbing Russia's ability to prosecute its war against Ukraine. "I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver is in the national interests of the United States," Trump wrote in Friday's order.The House passed the Russia sanctions bill on Sept. 16, and Trump signed it into law two days later. The bill was introduced over a year ago, and its primary backer was the late Lindsey Graham, a veteran Republican senator who represented South Carolina.Titled the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, the legislation targeted Russia's economy, intending to penalize the country over its continued full-scale invasion of Ukraine.The act required the president to increase duties on all Russian goods imported into the U.S. by up to 500% no later than 30 days after enactment. It also required Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries including China and India that are among the top five purchasers of Russian crude oil or gas. Trump's latest order waives these two parts of the Graham Act and comes two days before the law's implementation deadline. However, the order preserves existing sanctions on Russia under earlier executive orders.The law could also sanction Russian leaders, officials, and financial institutions, and expand sanctions on Iran. Oil sales revenue is critical to funding Russia's war effort.The move also comes a week after the Trump administration temporarily waived sanctions on Russian diesel exports through April 2027 to ease a supply crunch caused by the war in Iran.High fuel prices are a sensitive issue for voters ahead of midterm elections on Nov. 3. Trump's Republican Party holds a narrow majority in both chambers of Congress.A 'historic moment'"The suspension of some of the provisions of the Graham Act marks an important and truly historic moment," Kirill Dmitriev, Russian President Vladimir Putin's economy envoy, said in a post on X."The U.S.-Russia economic dialogue and peacemaking efforts will continue," Dmitriev added.But Trump's opponents have criticized the move.Sen. Richard Blumenthal, a Connecticut Democrat who also drafted the Graham Act, condemned the latest waiver."Donald Trump confirms again that he stands on the side of a bloodthirsty thug & the enablers of Russia's war machine & against the majority of Americans, their representatives in both houses of Congress, & our European allies," Blumenthal said in an X post.BRUSSELS, BELGIUM - OCTOBER 16: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy holds a press conference during the second day of the European Union leaders' summit in Brussels, Belgium, on October 16, 2026. (Photo by Dursun Aydemir/Anadolu via Getty Images)Anadolu | Anadolu | Getty ImagesSpeaking to reporters in Brussels on Friday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that the U.S.-Russia diesel agreement could set a precedent for further sanctions relief, while highlighting Ukraine's continued reliance on U.S. military technology and intelligence despite efforts to develop alternatives. "Sanctions will be lifted after gas," Zelenskyy said. "They will be lifted on something else. Then this will come to the banking system, certain individuals, chemical industry."Earlier this week, reports emerged that Ukraine has restricted SpaceX's Starlink military application, Starshield. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said in a post on X that the U.S. government and president were ultimately responsible for any curbs on the network.

schema.headline: Trump waives broad new Russia sanctions and tariffs under Graham Act, citing national interest

title: 'Everyone laughed' when he started a pumpkin farm—now it brings in $2 million a year
description: Three decades ago, when Kelly Schultz announced his intention to start a pumpkin farm, "everybody laughed at me," he says. Schultz, a second-generatio
body: Three decades ago, when Kelly Schultz announced his intention to start a pumpkin farm, "everybody laughed at me," he says. Schultz, a second-generation antique seller, had no prior experience with farming when he bought a small farm in Clarence, New York, in 1993.Nobody thinks he's out of his gourd now.Schultz, 74, is the owner and operator of The Great Pumpkin Farm, a seasonal attraction about 15 miles northeast of Buffalo that draws over 100,000 visitors each fall. The Great Pumpkin Farm brought in $2 million in annual revenue in 2025, according to documents reviewed by CNBC Make It — and it's open just seven weeks a year. This year, the farm is open to visitors between Sept. 19 and Oct. 31, and they're not just coming to buy pumpkins. With a $20 weekend admission ticket, fall enthusiasts can ride the farm's pumpkin-themed train, explore its giant corn maze and compete in pie-eating contests, among other attractions.Halloween is big business for Schultz and other seasonal business owners. Halloween-related spending is expected to reach $13.5 billion in the U.S. in 2026, according to a consumer survey by the National Retail Federation published in September. Among the 74% of Americans celebrating the holiday this year, 42% said they plan to carve a pumpkin.At The Great Pumpkin Farm, "attendance is increasing just about every year," according to Schultz.During the fall, "there are people that come here almost every weekend," he says. "They love it so much, they just keep coming back."A giant pumpkin put them 'on the map'Schultz, who runs an antique store and an antique auction business year-round, says he was inspired to start his farm after visiting a pumpkin patch in upstate New York in the early 1990s. That farm had "muddy parking lots and not a whole lot of restrooms," he recalls, but there were "a zillion people" walking around and buying pumpkins. "I looked around and I said, 'I could do this, better than this,'" Schultz says. So when the old cow farm next to his antique store went up for sale, he bought the 85-acre property for approximately $650,000, he says.With the help of other local farmers, Schultz learned how to grow his own gourds, and The Great Pumpkin Farm officially opened in 1996. But Schultz had even bigger plans for his farm. That same year, he asked Ray Waterman, founder of the World Pumpkin Confederation, an organization dedicated to growing giant pumpkins and squash, to host his annual World Pumpkin Weigh-Off at The Great Pumpkin Farm.Schultz bought prize indemnity insurance, which covers the cost of contest and promotion prizes, and offered $50,000 to anyone who brought in a pumpkin that weighed 1,000 pounds or more. He took out ads in papers "across the country" to promote the weigh-off. The winning pumpkin, grown by a couple from Lowville, New York, broke the world record at the time at a whopping 1,061 pounds.The Great Pumpkin Farm hosted its first pumpkin weigh-off in 1996. Courtesy of Kelly Schultz"We were in magazines and newspapers all over the world," Schultz recalls. "That put us on the map right off the bat." The Great Pumpkin Farm still hosts a weigh-off event every October, and this year's heaviest pumpkin weighed a whopping 1,908.5 pounds, almost double the weight of the 1996 winner.Hay rides, pumpkin cannons and moreThese days, Schultz focuses less on growing gourds — to keep up with demand, he purchases most of the farm's pumpkins from nearby farms. But The Great Pumpkin Farm's 50-foot pumpkin pyramid, which is visible from the road, is still the first thing that incoming visitors see. According to Schultz, the farm stocks over 25,000 pumpkins each year.Visitors pick out pumpkins to purchase at The Great Pumpkin Farm.William Muench | CNBC Make ItWeekend visitors pay $20 per ticket, which covers admission for both days. They can access a vast range of activities including hayrides, pie-eating contests, magic shows, a giant slide, live music, train rides, a kid-friendly "boo barn" and pumpkin pedal kart rides, just to name a few.For an extra fee, visitors can try the farm's amusement rides, pumpkin cannons, zombie paintball train, carnival games and Buffalo Bills-themed corn maze. Alongside the farm's bar and bakery, Schultz hosts festival food vendors whose offerings range from barbecue to specialty grilled cheese sandwiches."You can come out here and spend the day and still not have done everything," he says.Weekdays require no admission charge, and are more low-key. Visitors can purchase pumpkins, visit the Halloween store, bar and bakery, and enjoy the outdoor playground, petting zoo and hay maze. Schultz brings in petting zoo animals for the farm's fall festival.William Muench | CNBC Make ItCreating this fall festival requires a huge amount of labor, according to Schultz. He employs over 100 seasonal workers during the seven weeks the farm is open each year, and their job duties range from driving tractors for hay rides to serving pumpkin donuts.Rising gas costs are another major expense, Schultz says: It takes "lots and lots of gallons of fuel" to maintain the grounds and operate tractors for the hay rides. Since Schultz tries to avoid raising admission costs, he predicts that the business will "make a little bit less" in 2026. "The business has been profitable, but we generally take most of the money and try and put it back into it," Schultz says.For an extra admission fee, the farm also offers amusement rides and carnival games.William Muench | CNBC Make ItBecause Schultz owns the land surrounding the farm — approximately 300 acres in total — there's always room to expand, he says. Each year, he aims to add "something new, something fun, or upgrade what we already have."Creating a 'generational business'The farm has grown into a family operation: Schultz's son Ben has helped him run it, and his antique businesses, for the last 25 years."I just like hanging out with my dad, so that's how I got involved in all this," says Ben Schultz, 45. "I'm very proud of what he created here, and I'm just happy to be a part of it."Their shared goal for The Great Pumpkin Farm, according to Ben Schultz, is to "continue the momentum." From the farm's simple beginnings, "it's hard to imagine that it's gotten as big as it has," he says. Kelly Schultz's grandchildren have also started to help out around the farm, he says."They love coming here," he says. "They all want to be here all the time, every day." "I'm sure that the pumpkin farm will be a generational business," he continues. "It's definitely a family event."Kelly Schultz and his son Ben in front of The Great Pumpkin Farm's pumpkin pyramid.William Muench | CNBC Make ItThroughout October, the farm is buzzing with activity, but after Halloween, everything shuts down, according to Schultz. The petting zoo animals go back to their original farms; the amusement park rides are packed up and removed, and pig farmers pick up the remaining pumpkins to use for feed. Putting everything away and cleaning up the property takes approximately a month, Schultz says.For the rest of the year, around 20 full-time staff help maintain the Great Pumpkin Farm's old barn buildings and keep the grass mowed. Otherwise, it's back to selling antiques for Schultz and his family — at least until next fall.

schema.headline: 'Everyone laughed' when he started a pumpkin farm—now it brings in $2 million a year

title: Airport attacks put aviation in crosshairs of geopolitical conflicts
description: Surveillance footage shows people reacting amid smoke at the moment of an attack at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, October
body: Surveillance footage shows people reacting amid smoke at the moment of an attack at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, October 10, 2026, in this frame from a handout video.Saudi Ministry of Media | ReutersDeadly attacks on Saudi Arabia's second-busiest airport over the past week are highlighting how conflicts in the Middle East are upending air travel on a larger scale.Aviation is increasingly in the middle of these sprawling clashes as threats and outright attacks have forced airlines to quickly cancel flights throughout the Middle East for days, weeks and, in some cases, months. Some carriers might redeploy planes that would be going to some Middle East destinations like Dubai, United Arab Emirates, and Doha, Qatar, to other locations altogether."It's a new paradigm. Civil aviation is being directly targeted and it has not been the case in the last couple of decades," said Mark Zee, founder of OpsGroup, an independent aviation safety group whose members include pilots, dispatchers, airline employees and others. The Saudi airport attacks, claimed by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis, were the deadliest in the country in more than a decade. Over the weekend, at least 13 people were killed and more than 300 injured when a projectile hit terminals at King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh, officials said. Other attacks have included drones."Historically, airport security is focused on preventing unauthorized access to aircraft and the airport, not defending airspace," said Jeff Price, a professor at the Metropolitan State University of Denver's Department of Aviation and Aerospace Science and an airport management consultant.The threats to aviation are forcing officials to rethink how to protect blind spots in these major public spaces."There is this established way to deal with kind of more conventional weapons such as missiles. It's very expensive, but there is a way," said Gulnaz Ukassova, UAE-based security director of information and analysis at risk management firm International SOS. "There is still no sort of foolproof way to deal with the threat posed by drones. The technology, obviously, is constantly evolving."King Khalid International Airport has been shut down for much of this week, and some carriers suspended operations there, citing safety concerns. CEOs of major oil companies also pulled out of an energy conference in the country. Delta Air Lines, meanwhile, was less than two weeks away from launching an Atlanta-Riyadh route, the first nonstop commercial flight between the the two countries operated by a U.S. airline, according to the carrier.But late Sunday, the Federal Aviation Administration warned U.S. carriers about safety-of-flight risks when flying in or over Saudi Arabia. On Monday morning, Delta said it would postpone the route's debut until March. The new Delta route comes as Saudi leadership seeks to boost tourism to the country, part of the kingdom's Vision 2030 plan to diversify the economy from oil and attract international investment. Air traffic in Saudi Arabia had been increasing rapidly. Scheduled growth in airplane seats in the market is up more than 23% this year from 2023, though the rise has recently slowed, according to aviation-data firm Cirium.Whether travelers come back to the region depends on risk appetite. Ukassova said energy companies, which can depend on in-person visits to large projects, tend to have higher risk tolerance, while academics have a low bar for potential risks.Longer routes, cut flightsThe conflicts have cut off big parts of airspace in the Middle East, mainly over Iran. The outbreak of the Iran war in February set off massive aviation, travel and safety crises.For example, Australian carrier Qantas has changed its Perth, Australia-to-London route to avoid Iranian airspace. Because that flight is then longer, the carrier has added a stop in Singapore to refuel.For four years, Western commercial passenger and cargo planes have already had to fly longer routes to avoid Russian airspace. Carriers started detouring away from Russia after its 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Taking longer routes to avoid potentially dangerous airspace has been adding to airlines' fuel bills, which got even more expensive this year due to those same Middle East conflicts.While much of the traffic to Dubai and Doha has rebounded from the first days of the war since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28, it remains below 2025 levels, according to flight-data firm OAG. Capacity by seats across the Middle East is down 5.7% in October from last year, 2.2 million fewer seats, OAG reported.Some airlines are opting to stay away from the region altogether."We will not fly to Dubai and Doha, and we need to wait until the situation gets settled," Finnair CEO Turkka Kuusisto told reporters last month in New York. title: U.S. budget deficit swells to almost $2 trillion for fiscal 2026, up 12% in a single year
description: An electronic display shows the national debt in Washington, Aug. 19, 2026.Mandel Ngan | AFP | Getty ImagesThe U.S. finished the 2026 fiscal year with
body: An electronic display shows the national debt in Washington, Aug. 19, 2026.Mandel Ngan | AFP | Getty ImagesThe U.S. finished the 2026 fiscal year with a budget deficit of nearly $2 trillion, the latest measurement to underscore the extent of the country's financial stress. The $1.992 trillion figure was about 12% higher than the $1.775 trillion deficit in the prior fiscal year, the Treasury Department reported Friday.  It's the third-highest annual deficit in U.S. history, behind only 2020 and 2021, when the federal government was doling out trillions of dollars in financial stimulus amid the Covid-19 pandemic. The 2026 fiscal year saw record sums for both receipts and outlays, according to a Treasury Department official.With Friday's release, the U.S. officially recorded its 25th straight fiscal year operating at a deficit. The government last recorded a surplus — meaning its revenues were larger than debts — in 2001.Friday's report offers fresh evidence of how the U.S.'s fast-growing debt pile has dragged on the nation's overall financial health. The rising debt bill has helped exacerbate angst among bond traders, who sent the 10-year and 30-year U.S. Treasury yields to 24-year highs last week.Where the debt comes fromSocial Security amounted to the biggest slice of government spending at nearly $1.7 trillion for the full fiscal year, up modestly from the roughly $1.6 trillion spent in 2025.Medicare was the second biggest contributor, costing almost $1.1 trillion for the fiscal year. By comparison, the government-run healthcare program required slightly under $1 trillion in fiscal 2025.Net interest – a calculation of the Treasury's gross interest minus the interest it receives  – also topped $1 trillion for the fiscal year. In the 2025 fiscal year, net interest totaled $970 billion.Individual incomes taxes helped lessen the total deficit by bringing in more than $2.8 trillion, an increase of about 7% year over year. Corporate income tax provided $381 billion in receipts during the 2026 fiscal year. That was a decrease of about $70 billion from fiscal 2025 stemming from the tax cuts included in the One Big Beautiful Bill act passed by Congress last year.In the 2026 fiscal year, the U.S. shelled out more than $1.3 trillion in interest on the national public debt. The total owed exceeded $40 trillion earlier this year and has more than doubled over the last decade.  Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC in August that the U.S. can "grow our way out of" its increasing debt pile."Our message to our allies, our trading partners, is that global growth is the way to take care of this mountain of debt," Bessent said in August.President Donald Trump pitched his plans for broad and steep tariffs as a way to drive up revenue and shrink the government's debt. The White House has pushed forward with its strategy of increasing levies on trading partners despite the Supreme Court ruling earlier this year that many of those instituted by Trump were unconstitutional.The Treasury saw a record high for gross customs duties in the 2026 fiscal year, according to a department official. But the total revenue from customs took a hit due to refunds required following the Supreme Court ruling, which sent billions of dollars back to retailers.The Treasury also reported Friday that September's monthly deficit came in at $27 billion, a reversal from the prior year, when the department saw a surplus of $198 billion in the month.

schema.headline: U.S. budget deficit swells to almost $2 trillion for fiscal 2026, up 12% in a single year

title: Katie Zacharia out as Trump's White House press secretary
description: watch nowNew White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is leaving her job after just five days in the face of criticism over her performance, a White
body: watch nowNew White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is leaving her job after just five days in the face of criticism over her performance, a White House official confirmed to CNBC on Friday.Earlier Friday afternoon, President Donald Trump told reporters that he had just suggested to Zacharia that she quit."I just spoke to her about it. I said, 'Katie, is this for you?'" Trump said outside the White House."'If I were you, I'd reconsider,'" the president said he told Zacharia.The White House official, who asked not to be named in order to discuss the staffing shake-up, confirmed Fox News' report that Zacharia is "transitioning" out of the press secretary role.Zacharia's five-day tenure in the Trump administration is shorter than that of Anthony Scaramucci, who in 2017 served as White House communications director for less than 11 days. That length of time became jokingly referred to as a "Scaramucci" and was used to measure the durations of other officials who served briefly.By that metric, Zacharia lasted one-half of one Scaramucci."Records are made to be broken. But I take no pleasure in other people's pain," Scaramucci said in an X post later Friday.Zacharia, a conservative commentator who worked at Trump Media & Technology Group, had faced widespread criticism in the days since she led a short and shaky first press briefing. She also came under mounting scrutiny about her legal background.Trump spoke to reporters before heading to Georgia for a political rally as he hopes to boost Republicans' electoral chances with just 18 days until the midterms.But Trump's efforts to sell his agenda have been muddled in part by Zacharia, who ended her first, and only, press briefing on Tuesday after delivering halting remarks and taking questions from just three reporters.In the less than six minutes she spent answering questions, Zacharia revealed that U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle had been asked to step down. That departure, and Zacharia's, follow those of a number of other high-ranking female officials in the Trump administration who have quit or been fired in recent months."You know, she's been treated very rough. And she's a nice person," Trump said of Zacharia outside the White House.He accused the media of treating her "very badly" and said that even Fox News TV host Sean Hannity, a supporter of the administration, was "a little bit tough" on Zacharia during her appearance on his show Thursday night.Hannity, after calling Zacharia's debut briefing "widely panned," had asked about her past claims about her legal work in light of reports that she never passed a bar exam. Zacharia has defended identifying herself as a lawyer, drawing a distinction between that label and calling herself an "attorney."Hannity pointed out that Zacharia had called herself an attorney in multiple social media posts. "I think they were retweets, and I corrected the record," she replied.Trump called Zacharia "an attorney" in his Oct. 9 Truth Social post announcing her selection to replace Karoline Leavitt, who left the Trump administration in late August. Zacharia's first day was Columbus Day.White House officials had defended Zacharia earlier this week. "Up and down the White House, everyone has been thoroughly impressed with Katie in just a few short days on the job," White House communications director Steven Cheung said in an X post Wednesday. "At the end of this second term, she'll be remembered as one of the all-time greats," Cheung wrote.CNN chief White House correspondent Kaitlan Collins, however, reported Friday that Trump was "embarrassed by the coverage of Zacharia's briefing and when he polled other aides about her, Zacharia had few allies willing to stand up for her or defend her performance.""She's been treated, I would say, pretty nastily," Trump said of Zacharia in Friday's remarks outside the White House. "And I said to Katie just two minutes ago, I said, 'Katie, you know, you don't have to do this if you don't want.'"Asked if he would keep her in the role, Trump said, "I'm going to let her make that decision."

schema.headline: Katie Zacharia out as Trump's White House press secretary

title: OpenAI Saudi national bugging case shows threat to U.S. leadership in AI: DNI Clayton
description: watch nowU.S. companies and the Trump administration both "need to be wary" of foreign espionage attempts as the race for artificial intelligence domi
body: watch nowU.S. companies and the Trump administration both "need to be wary" of foreign espionage attempts as the race for artificial intelligence dominance continues, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNBC on Friday.AI "amplifies" existing cybersecurity risks toward U.S. digital infrastructure, which is interconnected with critical systems related to everything from public goods to the national defense and global communications, Clayton said on "Squawk Box."It's "why we're focused on hardening those systems" and using "our commitment to continue to lead to stay ahead of those nefarious actors," said Clayton, who leads a new White House AI task force.Clayton was asked how concerned Americans should be with the threat of foreign spying in light of the recently revealed case charging Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan with allegedly installing a recording device in an OpenAI executive conference room. Alfozan has not been charged with espionage; the federal charge involves alleged interception of oral communications.Alfozan, who was an OpenAI employee, had booked a one-way plane ticket to Saudi Arabia with his wife and another family member prior to his arrest, according to federal prosecutors."The short answer to your question is espionage, both commercial espionage, and I would say state-sponsored espionage, are realities," Clayton said."It's something that our private sector companies need to be wary of. We, as a government, need to be wary of," he said. The OpenAI incident "shows the lengths that people will go to try and supplant our leadership in this, or at least stay close to us in this emerging technology," Clayton said.An ex-CIA official, who asked not to be named because they were discussing information that is not public, told CNBC this week that the case is "probably the tip of the iceberg."Clayton, who was appointed AI czar earlier this month, said that the task force's "very good" inaugural meeting at the White House on Thursday built on the accord signed by President Donald Trump and a number of AI leaders at the White House last month. Trump had described the agreement, which includes industry pledges to police AI risks itself, as "morally binding."The task force also established three subcommittees that are focused on different AI-related issues. One is tasked with reporting and response, another with assessing critical infrastructure and working with the private sector, and a third with law enforcement and responsibility, Clayton said.The DNI reiterated to CNBC that the Trump administration is intent on staying ahead in the AI race."We're not the only ones developing it. There are vectors in this technology that are coming from some of our known adversaries and competitors," he said. "The Chinese, the Russians, the Iranians, the North Koreans all have significant technical capability. We need to stay ahead of them."

title: Trump's student loan overhaul could lead to more bankruptcy filings, former judge says
description: A sign points to the U.S. Bankruptcy Court in Lower Manhattan, New York City.400tmax | Istock Unreleased | Getty ImagesIn Judge Sarah Sharer Curley's
body: A sign points to the U.S. Bankruptcy Court in Lower Manhattan, New York City.400tmax | Istock Unreleased | Getty ImagesIn Judge Sarah Sharer Curley's nearly three decades presiding over bankruptcy cases, some were especially painful to witness, she said — such as the 73-year-old woman who stood before her in 2012 with a student loan balance of more than $584,000. The debt dated back to the 1970s and had grown throughout the woman's public sector career, Curley writes in her new book, "The Price of Forgiveness: Debt, Bankruptcy, and the Future of Fairness in America." She had "never made a lot of money," Curley said, and by the time she sought debt relief, the woman was living in poverty, with Social Security as her only income. Even so, strict bankruptcy laws can make it nearly impossible to discharge student loans. Curley, the first woman appointed to the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of Arizona, said it was a familiar story. "We allow the financial markets to take innumerable risks, yet we refuse to allow an individual to be forgiven for choosing to pursue an advanced degree," Curley wrote. Read more CNBC personal finance coverageCNBC's No. 1 financial advisor takes a family-office approachTrump Accounts hit 70 million enrolled and can now accept stock donationsThousands of homeowners face ARM resets — and much higher paymentsSocial Security Administration announces 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment for 2027CNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 rankedCNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026Curley retired in 2014. CNBC spoke with her this month about her new book, in which she describes a legal system that often fails to give indebted Americans the second chance it promises. In 2025, more than half a million personal bankruptcy cases were filed — an almost 50% rise from three years prior, according to the Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts.The interview has been edited and condensed for clarity. 'People are subject to many unexpected events'Annie Nova: What do people get most wrong about those who file for bankruptcy? Sarah Sharer Curley: People assume that individuals who file for bankruptcy are committing fraud, trying to hide assets and cheating creditors. Nothing could be further from the truth.  AN: And so why did people end up in your court? SSC: People are subject to many unexpected events. People can't always plan adequately for the next earthquake, hurricane or natural disaster. But usually, it's someone losing a job. It could also be an illness that becomes chronic with medical costs that increase dramatically over a short period. Student loans is another area of concern. Universities are charging more for basic degrees, as well as graduate programs. The cost of medical school over four years can be more than $400,000.  Sarah Sharer CurleyEverardo Keeme, Photo Fusion StudioAN: You write that many people who file for bankruptcy are not unemployed; they're just living paycheck to paycheck. What does this tell us about our economy and labor market? SSC: Despite the increase in wages that most economists tout, many people are working as independent contractors. They receive few benefits and have few rights. The company is not responsible to them. Other individuals may be working for a company but find the wages or benefits are insufficient. Many people are forced to work for several employers to meet their needs on a weekly basis. Although unemployment may be low, the quality of the employment is also low.  'I found her credible'AN: The story in your book about the woman in her 70s with the six-figure federal student loan balance really stood out to me. What happened in her case? SSC: The federal government would not agree to any settlement. I was the one who would have to decide whether her debt would be discharged or not. But the case law I had to follow was not in favor of discharging student loan debts. So, I didn't have a lot of flexibility in granting her relief. However, I gave her credit for seven years of public service helping out troubled teens in San Diego County, since people who are in certain types of public service only have a 10-year repayment period. That meant that she'd need to repay the debt for just three more years. AN: Wow. Why wouldn't the federal government agree to any settlement with her? SSC: The federal government retains law firms to represent it in bankruptcy court, allowing the law firms to have a certain amount of discretion as to how to proceed. As a result, some law firms are aggressive in the positions that they take. In the case of the woman in her 70s, the law firm attorneys didn't believe her when she said she had no assets and was on Social Security. But the law firm did not do an adequate investigation. I found her credible.'Harder to reach a settlement' on student loansAN: Under President Joe Biden's administration, it reportedly became easier for federal student loan holders to get their debt discharged in bankruptcy. What's the current situation like? SSC: There were attempts by the U.S. Department of Education to work out repayment plans for student loan borrowers who could not repay their debts. There was also the possibility that the Education Department would agree to forgive at least a portion of the student loans. However, once the Education Department was gutted in 2025, there were few, if any, employees who could approve the debt modifications through one of the offered programs. As a result, it has become harder to reach a settlement with the Department of Education. Lauren Harms, Intrepid LiteraryAN: In your book, you describe President Donald Trump's "big beautiful bill," which passed in July 2025, as an "attack" on student loan borrowers. How so? Do you expect the new law to drive up bankruptcy filings?  SSC: The bill created unrealistic federal loan caps for students. As a result, if a student takes out a loan from a private financial institution that's not federally guaranteed, that loan will often be provided at a higher interest rate. Let's say the student needs a $300,000 loan to go to medical school. If the individual has a lower credit score, their interest rate may jump to 16%, leading to a payment of $5,017 per month over 10 years, or $302,040 in interest. These expenses are not sustainable for most individuals. The rate of bankruptcy filings will most likely increase. Many bankruptcy filers 'feel they have failed'AN: You write that medical debt is another major reason people need to file for bankruptcy. Can you say a little more about this? SSC: There were many individuals who appeared before me who had chronic illnesses. Chronic diseases are a problem because the person can only discharge the debt they owe at the beginning of the bankruptcy case. As with any chronic illness, the debt continues to mount day by day for years to come. Many individuals are traumatized when they file a bankruptcy case. Sarah Sharer Curley Former U.S. Bankruptcy Court judgeAN: You write that the bankruptcy process is "tortuous" for most individuals. How so?SSC: Dramatic changes were made to the bankruptcy law in 2005. People are required to jump through many hoops to get relief now. There was no evidence to support certain beliefs that individuals were engaged in fraud or filing bankruptcy cases every few months. But the creditor lobby pushed to make the bankruptcy law more pro-creditor. The many forms that need to be filled out and the hearings that need to be attended usually keep the individual in a perpetual state of stress.   AN: How does filing for bankruptcy affect people emotionally?  SSC: Many individuals are traumatized when they file a bankruptcy case. They had believed if they just work harder, they could solve their debt problems. However, when they're about to lose their homes, their cars or their businesses, they turn to bankruptcy. Many see their inability to solve their financial problems as a moral failure. They feel they have failed. AN: What was it like for you, day after day, seeing people under the pressure of insurmountable debt? SSC: At times, at the end of the hearing, after I had rendered my decision, I would let the individual know that under the current law, I couldn't provide them with what they really needed. I told them that the law needed to be changed. We give a break to large financial institutions and corporations, and it's time that we do so for individuals, too.

schema.headline: Trump's student loan overhaul could lead to more bankruptcy filings, former judge says

title: Trump says White House didn't order Starlink restrictions in Ukraine
description: U.S. President Donald Trump speaks to reporters as he departs the White House on October 16, 2026 in Washington, DC. Andrew Harnik | Getty ImagesPresi
body: U.S. President Donald Trump speaks to reporters as he departs the White House on October 16, 2026 in Washington, DC. Andrew Harnik | Getty ImagesPresident Donald Trump on Friday denied that the White House had ordered restrictions this week on Starlink satellite internet services provided to Ukraine's armed forces.Ukrainian officials on Tuesday and Wednesday said SpaceX had restricted use of Starshield, a military-grade version of Starlink, without warning, impeding some military operations and its ability to defend civilians against intensifying attacks by Russia.SpaceX CEO Elon Musk pinned responsibility for any restrictions on the U.S. government and Trump, writing on X that, "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government."Reporters in Washington, D.C., on Friday asked Trump who was responsible for pausing access for the Ukrainian military. "Well, I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon," Trump said. "And from what I understand, it's the same as it's always been."Read more CNBC tech newsApple's $1,999 iPhone Duo puts the company's status-symbol power to the testTrump says White House didn't order Starlink restrictions in UkraineBlue Origin plans $330 million Florida expansion to ramp New Glenn launchesSpaceX AI policy leader grilled by NYC Council on Grok safety, sexualized imagesUkrainian forces have long relied on Starlink and Starshield to enable data gathering by their autonomous drones and for other communications. The restrictions cut off connectivity for drones or other vehicles traveling above 160 kilometers per hour.Serhii Beskrestnov, an advisor to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote in a post on Telegram this week that, "Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions, and this led to the failure of a number of missions." Radoslaw Sikorski, Poland's deputy prime minister, criticized Musk on X about the restrictions. Poland has purchased Starlink services for Ukraine from SpaceX."Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again?" he wrote. "As your European customers, we are watching you." Musk is an advisor to the Pentagon on technology through his role in the recently announced Project Meridian.The Telegraph reported Friday that Musk "approached Donald Trump with the idea of slowing down Starlink in Ukraine," and both had a hand in imposing the restrictions. Reuters reported on Thursday, citing two U.S. officials, that the call to restrict Starlink in Ukraine came from the White House, but did not say who made the order.On Oct. 10, after Trump called on Ukraine to stop all attacks on Russian oil refineries, Musk wrote in a post on X, "Zelensky has gone too far."Musk and SpaceX did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Friday.SpaceX shares are down about 11% this week. The company is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday. WATCH: Poland never underestimated Russia threatwatch now

schema.headline: Trump says White House didn't order Starlink restrictions in Ukraine

title: Tesla unveils long-delayed Roadster developed with SpaceX, fueling merger speculation
description: watch nowTesla showed off its long-delayed next-generation Roadster on Thursday, almost a decade after Elon Musk's company started taking deposits for
body: watch nowTesla showed off its long-delayed next-generation Roadster on Thursday, almost a decade after Elon Musk's company started taking deposits for the electric sports car. The event was livestreamed from a SpaceX test site in McGregor, Texas, near Waco, starting at 7:55 p.m. local time, or 8:55 p.m. ET. In attendance along with Musk were design leader Franz von Holzhausen and Lars Moravy, vice president of vehicle engineering."You're going to see some crazy stuff tonight," Musk said. "You're going to see the results of what happens when you have a collaboration with the world's best car company and the world's best rocket company."Tesla's original Roadster, designed and engineered by a team led by founding CEO Martin Eberhard, was based on a Lotus Elise chassis and was first delivered in 2008, selling for roughly $100,000 in small volumes until 2012.  Tesla unveils its long-delayed Roadster nearly a decade after first revealing a next-generation version of its original electric sports ​car, at a launch event in Waco, Texas, Oct. 15, 2026. In this still image taken from a handout video the Roadster comes to a landing using rocket thrusters.Tesla | Via ReutersThe next-generation Roadster is expected to be a high-end, low-volume model that relies on SpaceX technology to enable it to hover. While Musk fanatics expressed their excitement on social media, the Roadster isn't likely to have any material financial impact on the company.At the event, Musk and his team showcased a white sports car that raced up a curved ramp, then clung to it upside down and vaulted off it, flipping in mid-air and hovering slowly before landing on the ground.The two-seater can go from zero to 60 miles per hour in under a second, according to Tesla's timer, a feat Moravy demonstrated for the live audience.Musk said the next-generation Roadster would enter production in 2028. The price wasn't announced, and the company didn't disclose specifications about other performance-level variants of the new Roadster. It was unclear whether the vehicle would be street-legal, with Musk saying on stage that, "This is not necessarily a safety-optimized car."The Roadster unveiling has added to speculation of a possible merger between Tesla and SpaceX.For years, Musk's companies have worked with and paid each other, even sharing some personnel. The collaboration has increased in 2026, with speculation about a possible SpaceX-Tesla tie-up swirling since the aerospace and defense company went public in June. SpaceX COO Gwynne Shotwell told CNBC ahead of the IPO that a merger "might make Elon's life a little easier." Barclays analyst Dan Levy predicted in a note out this week that such a transaction could happen before the end of 2026.SpaceX is currently valued at about $2 trillion, while Tesla has a market cap of $1.4 trillion, making them two of just 12 U.S. companies worth at least $1 trillion. Tesla unveils its long-delayed Roadster nearly a decade after first revealing a next-generation version of its original electric sports ​car, at a launch event in Waco, Texas, Oct. 15, 2026Source: TeslaTesla reopened reservations for the refreshed Roadster in recent weeks, accepting $50,000 deposits from prospective buyers in the U.S., Canada and China. Musk first promoted the refreshed Roadster concept at an event in November 2017, and the following June in a series of tweets. He wrote at that time, "SpaceX option package for new Tesla Roadster will include ~10 small rocket thrusters arranged seamlessly around car." The engines would improve speed and braking, and may "even allow a Tesla to fly."The prototype Tesla showed on Thursday is built to be as lightweight as possible with a steer-by-wire system, steering yoke, and an array of technologies developed by SpaceX, including thrusters, carbon overlay pressure vessels and diffusers, and powerful fans that enable the car to do some gymnastics. One feature Tesla left out of its forthcoming Roadster is the company's "FSD" or automated driving system. Musk said the new Roadster will be the last vehicle the company produces that's intended to be controlled by a human driver.Tesla started taking $50,000 deposits for the revamped Roadster in 2017, but has since missed every targeted delivery date. As recently as last October, Musk was hyping a Roadster demo that he hoped would happen before the end of 2025. That didn't take place either. Tesla unveils its long-delayed Roadster nearly a decade after first revealing a next-generation version of its original electric sports ​car, at a launch event in Waco, Texas, Oct. 15, 2026Source: TeslaMusk's former friend and OpenAI co-founder Sam Altman mocked the Tesla CEO in posts on X last year over the extreme delays, showing screenshots of his reservation and refund requests. "I really was excited for the car! And I understand delays," Altman wrote. "But 7.5 years has felt like a long time to wait." Altman got his refund, and the two ended up in court earlier this year over a separate matter related to OpenAI's governance and ownership structure. Others have kept their reservations. Lawrence O'Connor, founder and CEO of Other World Computing in Austin, Texas, told CNBC ahead of the event that he reserved a Founder's Edition of the new Roadster in November 2017, effectively giving the company what he called an "interest-free loan" of $250,000. O'Connor wrote in a message that he would be attending the show and was "excited to see what has been 9 years in the making." After the event, O'Connor said what he saw was "off the charts."Tesla is scheduled to report third-quarter results after the bell on Wednesday.WATCH: Tesla Roadster unveil set for Thursday eveningwatch now

schema.headline: Tesla unveils long-delayed Roadster developed with SpaceX, fueling merger speculation

title: 5 midterm money takeaways: Democrats have candidate cash. Republicans have Elon Musk
description: A voter casts his ballot during early voting at the Polk County Election Office on Oct.14, 2026 in Des Moines, Iowa. Charlie Neibergall | Getty Images
body: A voter casts his ballot during early voting at the Polk County Election Office on Oct.14, 2026 in Des Moines, Iowa. Charlie Neibergall | Getty ImagesOne of the last big campaign-finance snapshots before the Nov. 3 Election Day is now available, and both political parties found something to like. But campaign cash is flowing in very different ways — and, on balance, points to an environment more favorable for Democrats.On one side, Democratic candidates have turned into absolute cash cows, raising oodles more than their Republican rivals across Senate and House battlegrounds.Republicans, however, still have a leg to stand on from an unprecedented flood of outside super PAC cash, bankrolled by a tiny circle of billionaires led by Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. The deluge of capital could be enough to stave off the worst of what has otherwise been a treacherous political environment for the GOP amid stubbornly high inflation and drooping approval ratings for President Donald Trump.A flurry of Federal Election Commission filings Thursday at a key deadline detailed what candidates raised and spent from July through September and give insight into many of the outside groups backing them. More of the outside-money picture comes next week with another deadline for additional filings. Here are CNBC's five takeaways:Democratic grassroots strength If Democrats want a financial case for a blue wave, start with the candidates themselves.Democratic Senate nominees put up gaudy third-quarter totals. James Talarico raised $60.2 million in Texas, Jon Ossoff brought in $33.1 million in Georgia and Abdul El-Sayed raised $30.7 million in Michigan. Sherrod Brown brought in $23.1 million in Ohio, while Troy Jackson raised $20.4 million in Maine, Mary Peltola $14.1 million in Alaska and Roy Cooper $12.2 million in North Carolina.Even in reliably red Kansas, Democrat Adam Hamilton raised $9.4 million.In several of those races, the Republican numbers were not even close. Ken Paxton raised about $10.2 million in Texas, Mike Rogers $9.7 million in Michigan, Susan Collins $5.2 million in Maine and Jon Husted $4.8 million in Ohio.Candidate dollars are especially potent in the final stretch because campaigns control where they go and qualify for lower television advertising rates than super PACs do. In other words, Republicans may be able to make up a $1 fundraising gap with outside money — but it can cost them more than $1 to do it.The same fundraising edge stretches into the House.Democratic candidates outraised their Republican opponents through September in 13 of the 21 House races currently rated Toss Up by Cook, according to a CNBC analysis of FEC filings. In North Carolina's 11th District, for example, Democrat Jamie Ager raised $2.1 million in the third quarter, compared with roughly $313,000 for Republican Jennifer Balkcom. The fundraising surge coincides with a shifting map: the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter projected last week that Democrats could gain two to six Senate seats — enough to put the four-seat majority threshold within reach — and nine to 19 House seats, which would flip the chamber.Republicans' ace in the holeWhile Democratic candidates dominate direct donations, Republicans are countering with overwhelming outside spending.The Senate Leadership Fund, the GOP's main Senate super PAC, raised a record $272.9 million from July through September, roughly $122 million more than its Democratic counterpart, according to FEC filings. On the House side, the Congressional Leadership Fund raised a record $94.4 million during the quarter and entered October with $156 million in cash, according to its FEC filing.That outside money is functioning as a financial backstop for GOP candidates who trail badly in direct fundraising. Texas is the most extreme example: the SLF funneled $158 million into Texas PAC, the super PAC backing Paxton, according to FEC filings. Elsewhere, Republicans have committed $15 million through the SLF to defend Sen. Pete Ricketts in Nebraska, The Wall Street Journal reported this week. Outside groups account for roughly 80% of all ad buys in Alaska, where the SLF has spent $14 million backing Sen. Dan Sullivan, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data.The blitz allowed Republicans to hold an aired-ad advantage in seven of eight top Senate battles and 25 of 42 contested House seats rated "Toss Up" or "Lean" Republican or Democrat by the Cook Report as of Oct. 9, according to AdImpact.But polls have shown little movement in recent weeks, despite the advantage.Elon Musk, chief executive officer of Tesla Inc., during the launch of America.gov in Washington, DC, US, on Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026. Daniel Heuer | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesMusk fights for TexasNo donor better captures the scale — or the leverage — of that outside-money advantage than the world's richest person, Musk.He pumped more than $276 million into federal political groups during the third quarter, making him the biggest known individual donor of the midterms. His disclosed giving included $158 million to Senate Leadership Fund and another $89 million to his America PAC, according to FEC filings. Most of that capital was earmarked for a single rescue mission: Texas, the state that's his primary residence and headquarters of his businesses.Musk gave the SLF $75 million on Sept. 9 and another $83 million on Sept. 23. Both times, the SLF transferred the exact same amount to Texas PAC the following day. The group, which is backing Paxton, reported no other donors through the end of September.Until now, many national Republicans had been reluctant to sink resources into the Lone Star state's expensive media market while fighting across an already expanded Senate map. Musk effectively erased that trade-off, supplying enough money to build a dedicated financial firewall around Paxton without forcing the party to pull resources from other battlegrounds.Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, a Republican candidate for the U.S. Senate, speaks to attendees during a campaign rally at Matt's Rancho Martinez on Tuesday, May 19, 2026, in Allen.Elías Valverde II | The Dallas Morning News | Getty ImagesDemocratic megadonors get off the sidelinesFor months, Democrats worried over the reluctance of traditional megadonors to write checks following the 2024 election cycle with presidential contest drama at the top of the ticket. The latest filings suggest that freeze is thawing — though much money is still bypassing the Democratic National Committee.Facebook co-founder Dustin Moskovitz and his wife, Cari Tuna, put about $16 million into the midterm fight this summer, according to FEC filings, while LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman, who had also withheld money from the DNC this cycle, poured $11.5 million into the super PAC backing Talarico earlier this year.The renewed megadonor money gives Democrats another source of firepower for the final weeks that can be quickly redirected if needed. Already, Democrats' Senate Majority PAC raised a record $151 million in the third quarter and ended September with $112 million in cash, even as its Republican counterpart raised substantially more.Record-breaking moneyAll the spending is feeding an election on track to shatter spending records.AdImpact projects $11.6 billion in political advertising during the 2025-26 election cycle, which would make 2026 the most expensive cycle on record — surpassing both the $8.9 billion spent during the 2022 midterms and the $11.2 billion spent during the 2024 presidential cycle.The congressional fight alone has already put $3.8 billion in advertising on the air, more than $870 million ahead of the comparable point in 2024, according to AdImpact. Senate races are helping drive the surge: the firm projects $3.4 billion in Senate advertising by the end of the cycle, up 48% from 2022.But as the amount of money rises, some of it is becoming harder for voters to trace back to its original source.Thursday's filings showed millions flowing into super PACs from nonprofits and other entities that are not required to disclose their own donors, leaving the original source of some of the cycle's biggest checks hidden.

schema.headline: 5 midterm money takeaways: Democrats have candidate cash. Republicans have Elon Musk
